The Gap

What existing metrics cannot see

Caltrans tracks delay, throughput, and crash outcomes. None of these capture what it is like to live next to a corridor running 20 mph above its posted limit every single day.

A road that is free-flowing can be free-flowing precisely because it operates too fast for its surroundings. That condition shows up nowhere in current reporting. SMP P.SA.01.20 asks Sustainability to change that.

What we currently measure
Crash outcomes

Mobility performance
What this work adds
Persistent speed exposure
Everyday conditions
System behavior vs community context
Upper-tail behavior
Safe Systems: Harm occurs when speeds exceed what surrounding human contexts can safely absorb. That is a quality-of-life burden independent of whether a crash has happened yet.
Methodology

From aggregated averages to actual observed behavior

Pre-processed speed metrics smooth out the upper tail. The core shift: use NPMRDS time-stamped individual observations, filtering directly for the 90th and 95th percentile readings that aggregation erases.

TierThresholdWhat it means on a surface street
Normal75 mph or belowWithin expected range
High75 to 85 mph, 1.3x postedElevated, concerning in residential context
Extreme85 mph or aboveDangerous regardless of context
Anomaly2x posted speed or more70 mph on a 35 mph residential street
Automated Pipeline

A scripted, reproducible workflow

We automate extraction, aggregation, and joins using Python, so the method can be rerun as data updates or scope expands to all 12 districts.

  • 1
    Extract high-speed observations from NPMRDS. Filter for greater than 90th/95th percentile passenger vehicle readings, April through September.
  • 2
    Aggregate to segment level. Count readings per speed tier per TMC. Capture frequency and time-of-day distribution.
  • 3
    Conflate to SHS network. 50ft buffer, spatial join, intersect, length-weighted P90 per SHS segment.
  • 4
    Cross-reference with StreetLight and Replica for validation and time-of-day patterns.
  • 5
    Overlay context layers: NLCD residential land use, CDE schools, EQI equity layer, bike and ped facilities. Compute exposure score. Generate hotspot map.
The QoL Lens

Speed alone does not tell the story. Context does.

A freeway at 70 mph is expected. An arterial at 55 mph next to a school is not. The exposure score combines the speed signal with who is actually exposed to it.

severity = (pct_anomaly x 2.0)
          + (pct_extreme x 1.5)
          + (pct_high x 1.0)
exposure_score = severity
                x lu_residen -- % residential within 500m
                x log(population/1000) -- how many people
                x 100, normalized 0 to 100
Anomaly weighted 2x because speed at 2x posted limit in a residential context is the most severe behavioral mismatch. Land use and population answer who is exposed.

Where the signal concentrates

1,278 SHS surface segments analyzed. Freeways shown in grey are explicitly out of scope for P.SA.01.20, which specifies surface facilities in developed areas. The surface arterial network running through the residential fabric is where this work focuses.

64%
of segments show zero excess speed readings

That concentration is a real finding, not a data gap. Excessive speeding is specific to particular corridors. That is what makes it actionable: specific places, specific interventions.

Critical Tier · Exposure Score 100

Madison Ave Eastbound

Two consecutive Critical-tier segments running through 37 to 50% residential surroundings with populations of 2,400 to 3,200 within 500 meters. 8.4% of all readings in the extreme or high tier across six months of data. Persistent, not incidental.

This corridor is free-flowing. No congestion, no delay flag, no performance alert in any existing Caltrans metric. It is free-flowing because it runs too fast for its residential surroundings. That is exactly the condition P.SA.01.20 was written to address.

High Tier · Anomaly Readings Present

Munroe St Southbound

0.77% of readings are anomaly meaning observed speed at 2x or more of the posted limit. Munroe St is posted 35 to 40 mph. Those readings represent 70 to 80 mph through a corridor that is 74% residential.

Median income $89k. This is not a low-attention corridor. The behavioral severity here, how far above design intent these readings are, makes this the sharpest single example in the dataset of what the anomaly tier flags.

Pattern · 6+ Consecutive Segments

Q St Corridor

No single Q St segment scores Critical or High. But six to eight consecutive segments each carry small, consistent anomaly readings. That is not noise. Something systematic is happening at the corridor level.

6+
consecutive Q St segments with anomaly readings

Combined population within 500m across these segments: over 30,000 people. The adjacent P St corridor shows the same pattern. A segment-by-segment view misses this entirely. A corridor view surfaces it immediately.

Corridor thinking matters. The ranked table enables this pattern to be seen. Individual segment scores alone do not.

Delivery Roadmap

Three items. One methodology.

This Sacramento pilot is the item a deliverable for 2026. The same pipeline scales statewide. Every district produces its own ranked table from the same code.

Item a
By 2026
Define and identify excessive speeding
  • Confirm reference speed definition
  • Join EQI for equity anchoring
  • Add posted speed limits, compute exceedance index
  • Extend pipeline to all 12 districts
  • Publish statewide ranked segment list
Item b
By 2027
Speeding abatement plan
  • District consultation on priority corridors
  • Policy framework: road diets, AB 43, lane narrowing
  • Programming path: SHOPP, HSIP, ATP
  • Publish official abatement plan
Item c
By 2028
Priority abatement project plans
  • Corridor profiles for top corridors statewide
  • Coordinate with PMP, CAT Plan process
  • Project plans published
